analysis.one_liner: Caps private-insulin copays at $35 a month and forces middlemen to pass insulin rebates to health plans.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the INSULIN Act: it sat in the Health committee from April 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025, so no $35 insulin cap took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what people with private insurance pay for a month's supply of insulin at $35 (or 25% of the drug's discounted price, whichever is lower), ban insurers from applying deductibles or prior-authorization hoops to covered insulin, and require pharmacy benefit managers to hand over every rebate and fee they collect on insulin to health plans. It would also speed up generic and biosimilar competition by cracking down on petitions filed just to delay rival products and fast-tracking review of biosimilars that face little competition. The bill was referred to the Senate Health committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who use insulin: their monthly cost would be capped at $35 with no deductible applied, no prior-authorization delays, and coverage even before meeting deductibles on catastrophic plans. Health plans also gain because PBM rebates on insulin must be passed through to them, and patients gain in the longer run from faster biosimilar and generic competition.

how_it_helps.text: Caps monthly insulin cost-sharing under private insurance at $35 or 25% of the net negotiated price, whichever is less, starting in 2025, with no deductible applied.
Requires PBMs and third-party administrators to pass 100% of insulin-related rebates, fees, and discounts back to health plans, within 90 days and subject to plan-sponsor audit.
Bars prior authorization and similar utilization-management hurdles on covered insulin unless clinically justified.

Tightens FDA review of petitions filed mainly to delay generic approval, refers abusive petitions to the FTC, and creates a fast-track for biosimilars facing little competition (fewer than three biosimilars on the market).

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators lose the fees and rebates they currently keep on insulin; health insurers bear the cost of the $35 cap; brand-name insulin makers face faster generic and biosimilar competition and fewer delay tactics.

drawbacks.text: The cap only applies to 'selected insulin products' chosen by each plan, so plans can cover one product per type and form at $35 while charging more for other insulins, and out-of-network insulin is exempt entirely.

Costs of the cap fall on health plans and employers, which could surface as modestly higher premiums for everyone rather than being borne by manufacturers, whose list prices the bill does not directly cap.

The generic-drug petition and Medicare formulary changes squeeze middlemen and tactics that delay competition, but industry groups could argue the new FDA dismissal rules and fast-track designations reduce procedural safeguards in drug review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill is well-targeted: the $35 cap directly relieves insulin users, the PBM rebate pass-through closes a documented channel where middlemen profit off insulin, and the FDA provisions attack delay tactics and slow biosimilar review. The costs fall on health plans and drug middlemen rather than taxpayers, and insulin is a small slice of total drug spending, so premium effects are likely modest. Weaknesses: the cap leaves plans free to designate which products count, allowing cost-shifting within the insulin category; the PBM provision is insulin-specific and does not fix the broader rebate system; and the bill contains no direct price caps on manufacturers, so underlying list prices stay untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP committee, which never voted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended without ever reaching the Senate floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 25, 2023 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died with it; any similar effort would have to start over in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and insulin makers are better off: the rebate pass-through, $35 cap, and competition provisions never became law, and the Senate never even voted.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its cap on insulin cost-sharing, PBM rebate pass-through, and generic-competition provisions.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Joined Shaheen in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan leadership from the start.

for.name: 13 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support in the Senate.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup in the 20 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: The chamber's majority-controlled schedule never took the bill up, since bills cannot reach the floor without leadership scheduling.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan: a Democratic lead sponsor, a Republican lead co-sponsor (Collins), and 13 cosponsors split 7 Republicans, 5 Democrats, and 1 Independent.

industries.note: The bill forces PBMs to hand over 100% of insulin-related rebates and fees to health plans and to disclose and allow audits of that money, cutting a revenue stream built on the spread between what manufacturers pay and what plans see.

Insurers must cap insulin cost-sharing at $35 and cover insulin before deductibles, raising their costs, but they also gain the rebates PBMs currently keep and relief from high-cost catastrophic claims. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the insulin patients the bill would help.

The bill speeds generic and biosimilar competition, restricts delay petitions, and would let insurers steer patients to cheaper biosimilars, eroding the pricing power that keeps insulin among the most profitable drugs.
The bill accelerates FDA review for biosimilars of products with fewer than three competitors and gives Medicare plans an easier path to swap in biosimilars, expanding their market.
